newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian feud forces Shell to reduce oil output.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian feud forces Shell to reduce oil output.

text.p: Fresh fighting in Nigeria's oil- producing Niger delta has forced oil giant Royal Dutch Shell Group to cut Nigerian oil output by more than 10 percent, oil executives said on Tuesday.
"Armed youths went to our Nembe creek fields on Sunday, disarmed the police on duty and asked us to shut down which we have done," a spokesman for the Nigerian unit of Shell told Reuters in Lagos.
Local newspapers said the latest outbreak of hostilities arose from an alleged seizure of relief materials to the community by one of the rival clans.
Shell has had to close many oil flow stations over the last two months because of protests by armed youths over a recent restructuring of local government areas.
In March it closed the same five Nembe flow stations, which together produce about 120,000 barrels per day of crude oil.
Nigeria's total output is about two million and Shell accounts for half of the production, which is mainly from the impoverished swamps.
Shell said the latest closures were, however, not affecting crude oil exports from the Bonny terminal, which is partly fed from Nembe.
"Exports are continuing normally at the Bonny terminal," the Shell spokesman said.
The oil-producing communities have long been restive because of their alleged neglect by the government and oil firms in an area that accounts for more than 90 percent of Nigeria's export earnings.
Shell last week commissioned a hospital it built in Nembe as part of its community assistance programme.
The Shell spokesman said the company was not directly involved in the latest flare-up.
"It is nothing to do with us. The group that came to our Nembe base is called Nembe Youth Camp. We are talking with Nembe elders or their reprentatives in order to restore normalcy," he said.
Another Shell official said :"We established contact with the youths and chiefs of Nembe yesterday and they were surprised about this. The dialogue suggests that we should be able to reopen soon."
Nembe is Ijaw-speaking in the recently-created Bayelsa state, where Ijaws, Nigeria's fourth largest tribe is the majority.
Ijaws in the midwestern Delta state, where Shell has its western division operation headquarters, have since March been fighting with the rival Itsekiri tribe in the oil town of Warri.
The fighting in Warri was triggered off by the relocation of the local council headquarters from an Ijaw to an Itsekiri town.
Troops have been stationed in Warri for more than two weeks now to end the fighting but occasional clashes have continued to break out in nearby areas.
Tribal clashes are common in Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation of 100 million and the continent's leading oil producer.
